summaries.example: Imagine someone reading a story and asking, “What is the writer trying to teach?” Kaspi did this with the Bible. He also used logic, or careful rules for thinking, to check whether an explanation really followed from the words. If a sentence says there was no one to farm the ground, Kaspi warned that this does not automatically mean there were no people at all.
summaries.summary: Joseph Kaspi lived in the Middle Ages and wrote many works about the Bible. He saw himself mainly as a commentator: someone who tries to explain what a text means. To do this, he used philosophy and logic. He believed logic could guide correct thinking and help people use language properly. He also studied Hebrew words. He argued that Hebrew words were not chosen randomly and that words that seem alike may still point to different features of an object or idea. Kaspi had a naturalistic view of many religious questions. He explained miracles as unusual events that may still have natural causes, rather than as events outside all nature. He also taught that education and wisdom were important for living well. His ideas were unusual, and many of his writings remained in manuscripts instead of becoming widely known.
key_ideas: Joseph Kaspi was a medieval Jewish thinker who mainly explained the Bible.
He believed philosophy could help readers understand biblical writing.
He wrote about logic, Hebrew words, grammar, theology, and good living.
He thought an explanation should make sense, even when we cannot be completely sure what the original writer intended.
Many of his works were never printed, and some were lost.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kaspi shows that studying religion, language, and philosophy can be connected. His work also reminds us that understanding a text takes care: readers should examine words, reasoning, and different possible meanings. His story teaches us that a thinker’s influence can be limited when writings are not published or preserved.

important_terms.definition: A careful explanation of a written text, especially a Bible passage.
Rules that help us think clearly and notice whether an argument makes sense.
The study of how words and languages work.
A book that explains words and their meanings.
A person’s understanding of what a writer meant.

questions_to_think_about: How can careful thinking help us understand a story?
Can one passage teach more than one lesson?
Should a dictionary explain why different words are used?
Why might an important writer be forgotten if many of his books are hard to find?

summaries.example: Consider the claim, “There was no person to cultivate the ground.” A careless reader might infer that no human beings existed. Kaspi treats that inference as invalid: the statement may concern the absence of farmers or cultivation, not the existence of humanity. This example captures his larger method—logical analysis should prevent interpreters from adding conclusions that the wording does not entail.
summaries.summary: Joseph ibn Kaspi was a fourteenth-century Jewish philosopher and biblical commentator whose work joins Aristotelian philosophy to the interpretation of Scripture. He wrote roughly thirty works, including commentaries, supercommentaries, logical treatises, theological discussions, and studies of Hebrew. His surviving corpus is incomplete: some works remain in manuscript and others appear to have disappeared. Kaspi regarded himself primarily as a commentator, but he gave a qualified account of interpretation. A commentary should seek the text’s real intention, yet the interpreter may lack demonstrative certainty about that intention. An interpretation can still yield a genuine understanding for the reader, and coherence among its claims can support confidence without amounting to supernatural revelation. Logic, in Kaspi’s view, is not merely a description of how people happen to think. It provides standards for correct belief and a universal structure underlying language. He applied distinctions such as general and specific, essential and accidental, contradiction, and valid and invalid inference to biblical reading. His linguistic theory portrays Hebrew as an exceptionally meaningful language: roots unify their derivatives, and different lexical forms are not absolutely synonymous. Kaspi’s theology treats God, prophecy, creation, providence, and human choice in rational and largely naturalistic terms. He also recommends education, books, teachers, and family as supports for the pursuit of wisdom. His originality may have contributed to his marginal historical reputation, but the entry presents him as a significant link between medieval Jewish exegesis, philosophy, logic, and Hebrew language study.
key_ideas: Kaspi understood philosophy as a tool for biblical interpretation, while also producing independent works on logic, language, and theology.
He distinguished a commentary from an independent treatise: a commentary should aim at the text’s genuine purpose, although the interpreter may not be able to prove that purpose.
For Kaspi, logic governs both sound belief and the proper use of language; he therefore criticized commentators who ignored logical principles.
His theory of Hebrew held that words reflect features of what they signify and that apparently synonymous words emphasize different aspects of the same thing.
His theology was strongly Aristotelian and naturalistic: God is understood through intellect, the world is not treated as beginning from absolute nothing, and miracles receive natural explanations.
Kaspi joined rational education with a demanding account of human improvement, while also expressing concern for animals and criticism of sacrifice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kaspi is important for seeing how philosophical methods can shape the interpretation of religious texts without eliminating interpretive uncertainty. His work raises enduring questions about whether meaning belongs primarily to an author, a text, or a reader; how logic relates to grammar; and whether apparently supernatural events can be interpreted within a natural order. It also illustrates how publication history affects which thinkers become recognized: innovative ideas can remain obscure when works are unpublished, lost, or situated between established intellectual categories.

important_terms.definition: Interpretation of a text, especially an attempt to reach its author’s intended meaning.
A normative discipline that supplies standards for correct belief, inference, and language use.
The study of language, including word formation, meaning, and grammatical structure.
Kaspi’s view that a Hebrew root has a central meaning shared by its derived words.
Words with related meanings; Kaspi denied that Hebrew contains completely interchangeable synonyms.
The view that events described as miraculous may have natural causes that people do not understand.
The philosophical study of God, human beings, knowledge, choice, and the good life.
An interpreter’s account of what the writer or divine author meant by a passage.

questions_to_think_about: If an interpreter cannot prove the author’s intention, what kind of truth can the interpretation still possess?
Does logical validity guarantee that the premises of an interpretation are true?
Can two words refer to the same object while still having different meanings or emphases?
How does a naturalistic account of miracles change the way biblical narratives are read?
Could Kaspi’s unusual combination of philosophy and commentary help explain why he remained less famous than more systematic philosophers?

summaries.example: Suppose a friend says, “There was no student in the library to work on the project.” You would not conclude that there were no people in the building; the sentence may only mean that nobody was doing that task. Kaspi used a similar kind of logical caution when interpreting a biblical sentence. He wanted readers to separate what the words actually say from extra conclusions they might be tempted to add.
summaries.summary: Joseph Kaspi was a Jewish philosopher and Bible commentator who lived in Provence and Spain during the fourteenth century. He traveled to Egypt, wrote in several areas, and produced many works, although a number were never printed or have been lost. Kaspi’s main project was biblical interpretation. He believed philosophy could help explain Scripture, so he wrote about logic, Hebrew, grammar, and theology as well as individual biblical books. Kaspi distinguished a commentary from an independent work. A commentary should try to uncover what its author meant, but interpreters cannot always prove that they have found the author’s exact purpose. A reader may still gain a true insight from a passage, even when the author’s intention remains uncertain. Logic was central to Kaspi’s method. He used it to test arguments and to warn against drawing conclusions that do not follow from a sentence. He also thought logic revealed a structure shared by all languages. In his account of Hebrew, words are connected to the qualities of the things they name, and words that appear to be synonyms often highlight different aspects. Kaspi’s theology was influenced by Aristotle and Maimonides. He gave natural explanations of miracles and prophecy and tried to reconcile divine knowledge with human choice. For practical life, he recommended learning, books, teachers, and family as supports for wisdom.
key_ideas: Kaspi used philosophy as a set of tools for reading the Bible.
He thought a good commentator should seek a text’s meaning but admit when certainty is impossible.
He treated logic as a guide to correct thinking, not merely as a description of ordinary speech.
He believed Hebrew words carry meaningful clues about the things they name.
He explained many religious ideas, including miracles and prophecy, through nature, knowledge, and reasoning.
He valued education and wisdom, and he also criticized harming animals for sacrifice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kaspi’s work connects questions that students often study separately: How should we interpret a text? What makes an argument valid? How do words get meaning? How can people be free if God knows everything? His answers are historically specific, but the problems remain valuable because they encourage careful reading, intellectual humility, and attention to the difference between evidence and assumption.

important_terms.definition: Explaining a text by investigating what it means and what its writer may have intended.
A method of checking whether ideas and conclusions follow correctly from one another.
The study of words, grammar, and how language carries meaning.
A work that explains another work rather than presenting only the writer’s own independent argument.
The purpose or meaning a writer is trying to communicate.
The idea that unusual events can still have causes within nature, even if people do not understand them.
A word or group of words that names or points to something.
Words that seem to mean the same thing; Kaspi argued that Hebrew words usually differ in what they emphasize.

questions_to_think_about: Why should readers distinguish a text’s words from conclusions they add themselves?
Can an interpretation be useful even if we cannot prove it is exactly what the author meant?
Do words that point to the same object always have the same meaning?
What might be gained—and what might be lost—when miracles are explained naturally?
Why could a writer who worked between several fields be difficult to classify?
